questions.stem: Which of the following is an actinoid?
questions.explanation: Actinoids are the 14 elements from thorium to lawrencium in which the 5f subshell is being filled, and uranium (Z = 92) is one of them. Cerium is a lanthanoid with 4f filling, and hafnium and scandium are d-block elements.

optionRationale.1: Hafnium is a 5d transition element, not an inner transition element.
optionRationale.2: Scandium is a 3d element placed in group 3.
optionRationale.4: Cerium belongs to the lanthanoid series, where the 4f subshell is being filled.

questions.objective: Identify actinoids in the periodic table

questions.stem: Which d-block metal is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury has a completely filled 5d subshell and very weak metallic bonding because its d electrons do not take part, so it has a low melting point of about 234 K. It is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

optionRationale.1: Zinc melts at about 693 K and is solid at room temperature.
optionRationale.2: Cadmium melts at about 594 K and is also solid.
optionRationale.4: Silver has a high melting point of about 1235 K.

questions.objective: Recall physical properties of group 12 elements

questions.stem: When sulphur dioxide is passed through acidified potassium dichromate solution, the colour changes from orange to:
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide is a reducing agent and it reduces orange dichromate, in which chromium is +6, to chromium(III) ions, which are green. Sulphur dioxide is itself oxidised to sulphate in this redox reaction.

optionRationale.1: Blue is not a colour of any chromium ion produced here; hydrated Cr(III) is green or violet.
optionRationale.2: Pink is characteristic of hydrated manganese(II), not chromium.
optionRationale.4: Chromium(III) is coloured, so the solution does not become colourless.

questions.objective: Predict the colour change of acidified dichromate

questions.stem: Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts mainly because they:
options: have very low ionisation enthalpies only
show variable oxidation states and can provide a surface for adsorption
questions.explanation: A transition metal can change its oxidation state and so form unstable intermediates with reactants, and many also adsorb reactant molecules on their surface where bonds are weakened. These two features allow an easier path for the reaction.

optionRationale.1: Most transition metal ions are paramagnetic, and magnetism plays no role in catalysis.
optionRationale.2: Low ionisation enthalpy alone does not explain catalysis; it is the variable valency and surface adsorption that matter.
optionRationale.3: Completely filled d orbitals belong to Zn, Cd and Hg, which are not typical catalysts.

questions.objective: Explain why transition metals act as catalysts

questions.stem: The number of unpaired electrons in the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ion (atomic number 26) is:
questions.explanation: Iron has the configuration $3d^6 4s^2$. Removing three electrons takes both 4s electrons and one 3d electron, giving $3d^5$, in which each of the five d orbitals holds a single electron. There are 5 unpaired electrons.

optionRationale.1: 4 unpaired electrons belong to $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ with $3d^6$.
optionRationale.2: 6 is more than the number of d electrons that remain in Fe(III).
optionRationale.3: 3 would be the count for $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ with $3d^3$.

questions.objective: Count unpaired electrons in a transition metal ion

questions.stem: In the lanthanoid series from cerium to lutetium, the differentiating electron enters the:
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids are formed by the successive filling of the antepenultimate 4f subshell, which lies deeper than the 5d and 6s subshells. The 4f orbitals are filled from 4f$^1$ to 4f$^{14}$ along the series.

optionRationale.1: The 5f subshell is filled in the actinoid series, not the lanthanoids.
optionRationale.2: The 5d subshell holds at most one electron in a few lanthanoids, but it is not the main subshell being filled.
optionRationale.4: The 6s subshell already holds two electrons and is not the one being filled.

questions.objective: Identify the subshell filled in lanthanoids

questions.stem: Transition metals generally have high melting points because:
options: a large number of unpaired d electrons take part in metallic bonding
their atoms are very large with weak attraction
they have completely filled d subshells
questions.explanation: In the middle of a transition series the largest number of (n-1)d electrons are unpaired and join the ns electrons in bonding. This gives strong metallic bonds, so melting points rise to a maximum near the centre of each series.

optionRationale.2: Large atoms with weak attraction would lower the melting point.
optionRationale.3: Metals conduct because of free electrons; the lack of them would not raise the melting point.
optionRationale.4: Filled d subshells, as in Zn, give low melting points rather than high.

questions.objective: Relate metallic bonding to melting point in d-block

questions.stem: When solid potassium permanganate is heated strongly, the gas evolved is:
questions.explanation: On heating at about 513 K, potassium permanganate decomposes as $2\text{KMnO}_4\rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4+\text{MnO}_2+\text{O}_2$. Oxygen gas is released, and the solid residue contains green potassium manganate together with brown manganese dioxide. This is a standard laboratory way to obtain oxygen from the salt.

optionRationale.1: Chlorine is not present in KMnO4.
optionRationale.2: Hydrogen is absent from the compound, so it cannot form.
optionRationale.3: Nitrogen is not present in KMnO4.

questions.objective: Recall the thermal decomposition of KMnO4

questions.stem: Aqueous copper(I) ions are unstable and change to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and Cu. This happens because:
options: the hydration enthalpy of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is large enough to offset the second ionisation enthalpy of copper
copper has no tendency to form a +2 state
questions.explanation: The disproportionation $2\text{Cu}^+\rightarrow\text{Cu}^{2+}+\text{Cu}$ is favourable in water because the very high hydration enthalpy of the doubly charged ion more than makes up for the large second ionisation enthalpy of copper.

optionRationale.2: Copper commonly forms the +2 state; most of its aqueous chemistry is that of Cu(II).
optionRationale.3: Cu+ has a completely filled $3d^{10}$ subshell, not a half-filled one.
optionRationale.4: Cu2+ has $3d^9$, which is not a noble gas arrangement.

questions.objective: Explain disproportionation of copper(I)

questions.stem: Misch metal, used in making flints for lighters and in some magnesium alloys, consists of about 95% of:
questions.explanation: Misch metal is an alloy of lanthanoid metals, about 95 percent, with about 5 percent iron and traces of sulphur, carbon, calcium and aluminium. Its pyrophoric nature gives sparks, so it is used in lighter flints, and it is added to magnesium alloys.

optionRationale.1: Aluminium-magnesium mixtures are not misch metal.
optionRationale.3: Actinoids are radioactive and are not used in an everyday alloy like misch metal.
optionRationale.4: Copper with tin is bronze, a different alloy.

questions.objective: Recall the composition and use of misch metal

questions.stem: In the preparation of potassium dichromate from chromite ore, the ore is fused with sodium carbonate in excess air. The chromium-containing product is:
questions.explanation: Chromite, $\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4$, is fused with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ in free access of air, which oxidises chromium(III) to chromium(VI), to give yellow sodium chromate, $\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4$. Acidifying this solution later forms sodium dichromate, which gives the potassium salt on treatment with KCl.

optionRationale.1: Sodium dichromate forms only after the chromate solution is acidified.
optionRationale.3: The oxidation by air raises chromium from +3 to +6, so Cr2O3 is not the product.
optionRationale.4: Chromium trioxide is formed on adding concentrated sulphuric acid to dichromate, not at the fusion step.

questions.objective: Outline the preparation of potassium dichromate

questions.stem: When green potassium manganate, $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$, is acidified, it undergoes:
options: disproportionation to purple permanganate and brown manganese dioxide
questions.explanation: Manganate(VI) is stable only in alkaline solution. In neutral or acidic solution it disproportionates: $3\text{MnO}_4^{2-}+4\text{H}^+\rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^-+\text{MnO}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving purple MnO4- and brown MnO2. One manganese(VI) species is oxidised to +7 while two others are reduced to +4.

optionRationale.1: Oxidation alone cannot occur without an oxidant; the same ion both gains and loses electrons.
optionRationale.2: Reduction alone to Mn(II) needs a reducing agent, which is absent.
optionRationale.4: A colour change from green to purple with a brown solid is clearly seen.

questions.objective: Describe disproportionation of manganate(VI)

questions.stem: The spin-only magnetic moment of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ (atomic number 28) in $\text{BM}$ is closest to:
questions.explanation: Ni$^{2+}$ has the configuration $3d^8$, which in a free ion has two unpaired electrons. Using $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$, we get $\sqrt{8}=2.83$ BM. This value is for the free ion, and strong ligand fields in some complexes can lower the number of unpaired electrons and hence the moment.

optionRationale.1: 3.87 BM corresponds to three unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.2: 4.90 BM corresponds to four unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.4: 1.73 BM corresponds to one unpaired electron.

questions.objective: Calculate spin-only magnetic moment

questions.stem: The equivalent mass of $\text{KMnO}_4$ (molar mass $158\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) when it acts as an oxidising agent in strongly acidic solution is:
questions.explanation: In acid solution $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, which involves five electrons per formula unit, and the equivalent mass is the molar mass divided by the electrons gained. The equivalent mass is $158/5=31.6\,\text{g eq}^{-1}$.

optionRationale.1: 158 would apply for a one-electron change to manganate in strongly alkaline solution.
optionRationale.3: 52.7 is 158/3, the value for reduction to MnO2 in neutral solution.
optionRationale.4: 79.0 is 158/2, which does not match any common reduction of permanganate.

questions.objective: Find equivalent mass from the change in oxidation number

questions.stem: Transition metals form a large number of complex compounds mainly because their ions have:
options: very large size and low charge
no tendency to accept electron pairs
small size, high charge and vacant d orbitals of suitable energy
questions.explanation: Small, highly charged ions attract ligands strongly, and the empty (n-1)d, ns and np orbitals can accept lone pairs from ligands to form coordinate bonds. These factors explain the wide range of complexes of the d-block.

optionRationale.1: Large size and low charge would give weak attraction to ligands.
optionRationale.2: Complex formation depends on accepting electron pairs from ligands.
optionRationale.3: Filled d orbitals leave no vacant orbitals for accepting lone pairs.

questions.objective: Explain complex formation by transition metals

questions.stem: In acidic medium, how many moles of $\text{KMnO}_4$ are needed to oxidise completely one mole of ferrous oxalate, $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$?
questions.explanation: Per mole of ferrous oxalate, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ gives one electron (to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$) and $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ gives two (to $2\text{CO}_2$), a total of three. Each $\text{MnO}_4^-$ takes five electrons in acid, so $3/5=0.6$ mol is needed.

optionRationale.2: 1.0 treats each KMnO4 as accepting three electrons.
optionRationale.3: 0.2 counts only the electron from Fe2+ divided by five.
optionRationale.4: 0.4 counts only the two electrons from oxalate divided by five.

questions.objective: Apply electron balance in permanganate titrations

questions.stem: $30.0\,\text{mL}$ of $0.100\,\text{M}$ sodium sulphite solution is oxidised to sulphate by acidified $0.100\,\text{M}$ $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, which is reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$. The volume of dichromate solution needed is:
questions.explanation: Sulphite loses two electrons per ion, so $3.00$ mmol of it gives $6.00$ mmol of electrons. One dichromate ion accepts six electrons, so $1.00$ mmol is needed, which in $0.100\,\text{M}$ solution is $10.0\,\text{mL}$.

optionRationale.1: 30.0 mL would result if the electron change of dichromate were taken as equal to that of sulphite.
optionRationale.3: 90.0 mL multiplies instead of dividing by the three-to-one stoichiometry.
optionRationale.4: 5.0 mL would correspond to twelve electrons per dichromate.

questions.objective: Compute a redox titration volume

questions.stem: $E^\circ(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+})$ is negative ($-0.41$ V) while $E^\circ(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+})$ is highly positive ($+1.57$ V). This is because:
options: both $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ have noble gas configurations
$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ has the stable $d^3$ configuration, and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ has the stable half-filled $d^5$ configuration
chromium and manganese have the same number of d electrons
questions.explanation: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ($3d^3$) has a stable half-filled $t_{2g}$ set, so $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ is a good reducing agent and the couple has a negative potential. $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) is very stable, so $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ readily gains an electron and is a strong oxidant.

optionRationale.1: Neither Cr2+ nor Mn3+ has a noble gas configuration.
optionRationale.3: The configurations are reversed: Cr3+ is d3 and Mn3+ is d4.
optionRationale.4: Cr and Mn differ in their number of d electrons, which causes the difference in potentials.

questions.objective: Relate electrode potentials to d-electron stability

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of lanthanoid ions is colourless?
questions.explanation: Colour in lanthanoid ions arises from f-f transitions, which need partly filled 4f orbitals. $\text{La}^{3+}$ has $4f^0$ and $\text{Lu}^{3+}$ has $4f^{14}$, so no f-f transition is possible and both are colourless.

optionRationale.2: Sm3+ is yellow and Dy3+ is yellowish, so this pair is coloured.
optionRationale.3: Er3+ is pink and Tm3+ is pale green, so they are coloured.
optionRationale.4: Pr3+ is green and Nd3+ is lilac, both coloured.

questions.objective: Relate f-electron count to colour of lanthanoid ions

questions.stem: Which of the following lanthanoid ions is most likely to be a strong reducing agent in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: The common and most stable oxidation state of lanthanoids is +3, so a +2 ion tends to lose an electron to reach it. $\text{Eu}^{2+}$ readily oxidises to $\text{Eu}^{3+}$, making it a strong reductant.

optionRationale.1: Eu3+ is already in the stable +3 state and does not act as a reducing agent.
optionRationale.3: Lu3+ has a filled 4f subshell and is stable in +3.
optionRationale.4: Gd3+ is a stable trivalent ion with no tendency to lose an electron.

questions.objective: Link unusual oxidation states with redox behaviour

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Transition metals have high enthalpies of atomisation.
**Reason (R):** They have a large number of unpaired d electrons that take part in strong interatomic bonding.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The more unpaired (n-1)d electrons an atom has, the stronger its metallic bonding, so the energy needed to atomise it is high. Hence the high enthalpies of atomisation of the transition metals. The reason therefore correctly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R directly explains A; it is not an independent statement.
optionRationale.3: R is true; unpaired d electrons contribute to bonding.
optionRationale.4: A is true; atomisation enthalpies of d-block metals are high.

questions.objective: Explain high atomisation enthalpies of d-block metals

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Many compounds of transition metals are coloured.
**Reason (R):** Transition metals have high melting points.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Colour arises from d-d transitions of unpaired electrons in partly filled d orbitals, which absorb visible light. High melting point is also true for transition metals, but it is due to metallic bonding and has no link to colour, so R does not explain A.

optionRationale.1: Melting point is a property of metallic bonding and cannot cause colour.
optionRationale.3: R is true; transition metals typically have high melting points.
optionRationale.4: A is true; many transition metal ions are coloured.

questions.objective: Distinguish the origin of colour from metallic properties

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** An orange solution of dichromate changes to yellow chromate when the solution is made alkaline.
**Reason (R):** Dichromate ions are more stable than chromate ions in alkaline solution.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The equilibrium $2	ext{CrO}_4^{2-}+2	ext{H}^+ightleftharpoons	ext{Cr}_2	ext{O}_7^{2-}+	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$ shifts to the left when hydroxide removes hydrogen ions, so orange dichromate gives yellow chromate. The assertion is true. The reason is false because chromate, not dichromate, is the stable ion in alkaline solution.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is not a true statement; chromate is the stable ion in alkali.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the orange to yellow change occurs in alkali.

questions.objective: Recall the pH dependence of chromate and dichromate

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** The atomic radii of the second and third transition series elements in the same group differ greatly.
**Reason (R):** The 4f electrons in lanthanoids shield the nuclear charge very poorly.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Poor shielding by the 4f electrons causes a steady decrease in radii across the lanthanoids, which offsets the usual increase in size going down a group. As a result the 5d elements, such as Hf, have almost the same radii as the 4d elements, such as Zr. The assertion is false and the reason is true.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so R cannot be its explanation.
optionRationale.2: A is false; the radii are very similar, not very different.
optionRationale.3: R is true; 4f electrons are poor shielders.

questions.objective: Link lanthanoid contraction to similar radii of 4d and 5d elements

questions.stem: Match the ion in List-I with its magnetic or electronic feature in List-II.
questions.explanation: $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ and diamagnetic. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3d^5$ with five unpaired electrons. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $3d^9$ with one unpaired electron, and $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ has no d electrons ($d^0$) and is colourless. So A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: Wrong: A belongs with III, not II and B belongs with II, not III.
optionRationale.2: Wrong: B belongs with II, not I and C belongs with I, not II.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: A belongs with III, not IV and D belongs with IV, not III.

questions.objective: Match ions with their d-electron features

questions.stem: Match the lanthanoid in List-I with its unusual oxidation state and reason in List-II.
questions.explanation: Cerium reaches +4 by attaining $4f^0$. Europium forms +2 with half-filled $4f^7$, ytterbium forms +2 with filled $4f^{14}$, and terbium forms +4 with half-filled $4f^7$. Therefore A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

optionRationale.2: Wrong: A belongs with II, not IV and D belongs with IV, not II.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: C belongs with I, not IV and D belongs with IV, not I.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: A belongs with II, not I and C belongs with I, not II.

questions.objective: Explain unusual oxidation states of lanthanoids

questions.stem: Match the condition for reduction of $\text{KMnO}_4$ in List-I with the manganese-containing product in List-II.

left: B. Neutral or faintly alkaline solution

questions.explanation: In strongly acidic solution permanganate is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, in neutral or weakly alkaline solution to $\text{MnO}_2$, and in strongly alkaline solution to green manganate by a one-electron change. On heating the solid it gives $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$, $\text{MnO}_2$ and oxygen. The code is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.1: Wrong: B belongs with II, not IV and D belongs with IV, not II.
optionRationale.2: Wrong: A belongs with I, not IV and D belongs with IV, not I.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: C belongs with III, not IV and D belongs with IV, not III.

questions.objective: Match the medium with the reduction product of permanganate

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the 3d series.
A. Most transition metal ions with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic.
B. Zn$^{2+}$ compounds are coloured because of d-d transitions.
C. Zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the 3d series.
D. Zn, Cd and Hg have the highest melting points in their series.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Unpaired d electrons make an ion paramagnetic in a magnetic field, and zinc has a $3d^{10}$ configuration with no unpaired d electrons for metallic bonding, so its atomisation enthalpy is the lowest. Zn2+ is colourless because it has no d-d transition, and group 12 elements have the lowest melting points, so B and D are false.

optionRationale.2: D is false because Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points.
optionRationale.3: B is false because Zn2+ is d10 and colourless.
optionRationale.4: B and D are both false.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on magnetism, colour and bonding in the 3d series

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about f-block elements.
A. All actinoids are radioactive.
B. Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
C. All lanthanoids are radioactive.
D. The 5f orbitals are less buried than the 4f orbitals and are more available for bonding.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: All actinoids are radioactive, and they show more oxidation states because the 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close. The 5f orbitals extend further than 4f, making them more available for bonding. Statement C is false because most lanthanoids are stable, and only promethium is radioactive.

optionRationale.1: C is false, since only promethium among lanthanoids is radioactive.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.4: C is false, and B is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Compare lanthanoids and actinoids

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about alloys of transition metals.
A. Transition metals readily form alloys because their atomic sizes are very different.
B. Steel is an alloy of iron with carbon.
C. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
D. Alloys are generally harder than the pure metals from which they are made.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Alloys form readily among transition metals because their atomic radii are similar, so atoms of one metal can replace those of another in the lattice. Statement A gives the opposite reason and is false. Steel is iron with carbon, brass is copper with zinc, and alloys are usually harder than their components.

optionRationale.1: A is false and B is true, so this option leaves out B.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so this option cannot be correct.
optionRationale.3: A is false.

questions.objective: Evaluate facts about alloy formation
